title: Publication and setting
short: From Harper's Poems on Miscellaneous Subjects (1854; enlarged 1857), published while she lectured for the antislavery cause; one of her best-known poems.
body: Frances Ellen Watkins (later Harper, 1825-1911), born free in Baltimore, published Poems on Miscellaneous Subjects in Boston in 1854 with a preface by William Lloyd Garrison; it sold widely and was enlarged in 1857. She had begun lecturing for the Maine Anti-Slavery Society in 1854, and she read from the book at her lectures. The poem belongs to the abolitionist literature of sentiment that followed Uncle Tom's Cabin (1852), which aimed to move readers by showing slavery's destruction of the family. Its scene is an auction or sale at which a mother loses her son.

anchor: Saw you those hands so sadly
title: Questions to the reader
short: The opening stanzas question the reader directly ('Heard you...?', 'Saw you...?'), forcing the audience into the role of witness.
body: Rather than narrating, Harper begins with the inverted questions of the oral ballad and the platform speech. Each stanza moves to a closer view: the shriek, the clasped hands and bowed head, then the 'imploring eye'. Critics such as Carla Peterson and Frances Smith Foster stress the connection with Harper's lecturing: the poem was meant to be heard, and it positions listeners as spectators who must respond. The stanza with 'She is a mother' (l. 13) then answers the questions.

anchor:
It rose
So wildly on the
title: Ballad metre
short: Quatrains of short ballad lines rhymed abcb (here 6.6.8.6 syllables), the measure of hymns and popular ballads.
body: The poem uses a variant of the hymn and ballad stanza, familiar to Harper's audiences from church singing: four lines rhymed on the second and fourth ('air/despair'). The opening stanza runs 6.6.8.6 syllables ('Heard you that shriek? It rose / So wildly on the air, / It seemed as if a burden'd heart / Was breaking in despair'), a little looser than strict common metre, and the pattern repeats through the poem. The simplicity was deliberate: Harper wrote for a broad public, including people who heard rather than read poetry.

sources.cite: Frances Smith Foster, ed., A Brighter Coming Day: A Frances Ellen Watkins Harper Reader (Feminist Press, 1990)

title: A storm of agony
short: The mother's mind is swept by grief as if by a storm; the poem uses intense, even melodramatic images to produce sympathy.
body: Harper's imagery here is that of sentimental and gothic fiction: the shriek, the 'shuddering' frame, the storm 'sweeping through the brain'. Some later critics found her verse over-emphatic; scholars from the 1980s on, notably Foster and Boyd, have argued that its directness was a political choice suited to an antislavery public that had to be moved to act. The mother is described entirely from outside, by what a spectator can see and hear.

title: kirtle
short: A woman's gown or skirt; an archaic word lending a ballad flavour.
body: Old English cyrtel, a tunic or short garment, later a woman's gown or outer petticoat. By the 1850s the word was archaic and literary, associated with old ballads and Scott's romances. Its use lends the plain scene a timeless, folk-ballad tone. The child hiding in his mother's skirts is an image of utter helplessness: the only protection he has is cloth.

anchor: He is not hers, although she
title: Anaphora: 'He is not hers'
short: Three lines across two stanzas begin with the same denial, building the poem's argument that slavery breaks the natural bond of mother and child.
body: The repetition (anaphora) works like a speaker's refrain. Each clause sets a natural fact (she bore him; her blood is in his veins) against the legal fact that he is not hers. The second stanza (ll. 21-22) explains why: 'cruel hands / May rudely tear apart' the family. The repetition gives an argumentative spine to a poem that otherwise proceeds by images.

anchor:
although her blood
Is coursing through
title: The law of slave birth
short: Under American slave law a child followed the status of the mother, so her son was born the property of her owner, not her own.
body: From a Virginia statute of 1662 onward, colonial and state laws applied the principle partus sequitur ventrem ('the offspring follows the womb'): children of enslaved women were enslaved and belonged to the mother's owner. The mother's blood in his veins thus makes the boy a slave rather than securing him to her, a bitter irony the stanza exposes. Enslaved families had no legal standing and could be separated by sale, the event the poem dramatises.

anchor: The only wreath of household love
title: Wreath of household love
short: The child is the circle that binds her life together; a wreath also suggests a crown and a funeral garland.
body: A wreath is a circle of woven flowers, so the image fits a bond that encircles and 'binds her breaking heart'. Harper uses a similar phrase in the companion poem 'The Slave Mother: A Tale of the Ohio', where the mother fears 'some cruel hand / Should tear my household wreaths apart'. The image anticipates the 'circling arms' of l. 33, which are torn open in the climax.

title: Fountain in the desert
short: The son is a spring of water in the wilderness of her life, an image with strong biblical resonance.
body: Isaiah promises that 'in the wilderness shall waters break out, and streams in the desert' (35:6) and that God will make 'the wilderness a pool of water' (41:18). Harper's audiences would have heard the echo: the boy's love is a providential blessing in the 'desert' of slavery. The following stanza continues the water imagery with 'a streamlet blent in one', so that the separation becomes the dividing of a single stream.

sources.cite: The Bible, Authorized (King James) Version, Isaiah 35:6; 41:18

title: blent
short: An old past participle of 'blend': their two lives were mingled into one small stream.
body: 'Blent' is a poetical form of 'blended', common in nineteenth-century verse. The image of two lives as one stream makes the coming separation unnatural: a stream cannot be torn apart. The diction, like 'kirtle' and 'No marvel', keeps the poem in the register of ballad and hymn. The word also echoes 'blood' and 'veins' earlier: mother and son are one life in body as well as in feeling.

title: 'Oh, Father!'
short: A sudden prayer to God, the heavenly Father, interrupting the narration; it also contrasts with the absent earthly father.
body: The apostrophe turns the poem from description to prayer and protest. 'Father' here is God, to whom the speaker (or the mother) appeals against the cruelty of men. Readers have noted that no human father appears in the poem: enslaved fathers had no legal rights over their children, and in many cases the father was the owner himself. The question is left unanswered by heaven; the next stanza simply reports the separation.

anchor: They tear him from her circling
title: The separation
short: The sale is completed; the mother will never see her son again.
body: The climax comes in a single stanza with no description of buyers, only 'They' and their violence. 'Circling arms' recalls the 'wreath' of l. 23, now broken. The wish 'never more may her sad eyes / Gaze on his mournful face' states what such separations usually meant in practice: family members sold apart were rarely reunited, though formerly enslaved people searched for each other for decades after emancipation.

title: Circular frame
short: The final stanza returns to the shriek and the 'breaking' heart of the opening, now explained: 'She is a mother'.
body: The poem ends almost where it began, repeating the rhyme 'air/despair' and the phrase about the breaking heart. What has changed is the reader's knowledge: the shriek of the first line is now understood. 'No marvel' means 'it is no wonder'. The repetition of 'She is a mother' from l. 13 makes motherhood the poem's appeal across racial lines, a strategy aimed especially at white women readers in the antislavery movement.
